ABUF: Four buffer funds staggered through the year, each absorbing the first 15% of S&P 500 losses over its own twelve-month period while capping gains. Laddering means protection renews quarterly instead of once a year, smoothing the risk of starting right before a drop or a rally.
ADVE: Dividend-paying companies across Asia, from Taiwanese and Korean tech manufacturers to banks in Singapore and beyond. It pairs Asia's growth with an income discipline, favoring established payers over speculative names, as a regional holding for investors who want yield from the world's fastest-growing region.
AFSC: A tight portfolio of roughly forty small US companies, spread across health care, banking, industry and technology. Focused means each pick matters: the managers hold only their strongest small-cap ideas, so the fund can beat or trail the small-cap pack by wide margins.
AGMI: Silver mining companies from around the world, from the biggest producers to smaller explorers betting on new deposits. Silver is both a precious metal and an industrial one used in solar panels and electronics, so the fund swings with investor fear and factory demand alike.
AMYY: An income strategy built on options tied to a leveraged fund on AMD, the chip designer, rather than on the stock itself. It sells options to harvest the fat premiums a fast-moving leveraged fund creates, aiming for large payouts while taking amplified losses when the chip stock slides.
ASGM: Futures contracts across world markets, stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, traded long and short by following macroeconomic trends. It is a hedge-style diversifier meant to zig when stock portfolios zag, especially in long market slumps, though trend systems can whipsaw in choppy markets.
BCCC: Bitcoin exposure built synthetically with options, paired with a covered call program that sells away part of the upside for current income. It pays regular distributions while still falling with bitcoin in sell-offs, suiting income seekers who know the cap cuts both ways.
BCGD: Established companies worldwide with durable advantages, the moats that let them keep growing through good times and bad, spread across technology, banking and consumer brands. Baron runs it as a long-term compounder portfolio, favoring proven global franchises over speculative growth stories.
BETE: Bitcoin and ether held through futures contracts in equal halves, rebalanced so neither coin dominates. Equal weighting gives ether, the smaller and often jumpier coin, a bigger role than market-size funds allow, and futures pricing can drift from the coins themselves.
BGRO: Large US growth companies picked actively by BlackRock's managers, with technology over half and media and industry behind. It plays the classic growth role, chasing companies expanding faster than the economy, with an active manager free to stray from the big growth indexes.
BGUS: US growth companies picked by a Scottish firm known for very long holding periods, led by technology at two-fifths. It hunts for the rare companies that can compound for a decade, so it is a patient growth holding that will lag when markets favor cheap, steady stocks.
COSW: Magnified exposure to a single stock, warehouse retailer Costco, built from swaps and shares, designed to pay distributions every week. Weekly payouts on one company is the whole appeal, and the leverage means it swings harder than Costco itself, a trading-style income tool rather than a holding to forget.
DADS: Debt rather than stock: bonds, convertible notes and preferred shares issued by crypto companies such as miners and firms holding bitcoin on their balance sheets. It aims for bond-style income from the crypto industry, trading the coins' explosive upside for steadier payments, though the issuers' credit rises and falls with crypto prices.
DWWN: Long-term US government bonds, the kind whose prices move the most when interest rates change. Long bonds pay higher yields and can surge when rates fall or recession fears grow, making this a strong but touchy defensive holding: a rise in rates hits it harder than shorter bonds.
ENHE: Emerging-market companies picked with return-forecast models, led by technology at about two-fifths and banks next, spanning Asia, Latin America and beyond. It is an actively tilted way to own developing markets, aiming to add a little extra over the big emerging-market indexes while keeping their well-known swings.
FDND: Internet companies, from online platforms and media to e-commerce, paired with an options program that targets a steady income stream. It tries to turn a growth-heavy corner of tech into an income holding, giving up some upside when internet stocks run hot.
FIXP: A model-driven mix of bond funds covering government, corporate and mortgage debt, with option overlays added to boost income. The model shifts between bond sectors as conditions change, so it plays an active core-plus bond role with an extra income engine most bond funds lack.
GEMQ: Emerging-market stocks chosen by Goldman Sachs using data-heavy computer models rather than old-fashioned stock picking alone. It aims for broad developing-world growth, from Asian tech to Latin American banks, with a quantitative edge, while keeping the currency and political swings those markets are known for.
INVN: Mid-sized US companies judged innovative but not yet fully appreciated by the market, led by technology at well over half and health care next. It is a growth hunt in the market's middle ranks, pairing Alger's innovation research with smaller, jumpier stocks than the mega-cap tech funds hold.
IVSI: Large companies in developed markets outside North America, in Europe, Japan, Australia and elsewhere, screened by a valuation system that estimates what each business is really worth. It is a value-tilted foreign core holding, favoring profitable firms priced below their estimated worth over fashionable growers.
JOUL: Companies that make the heavy equipment of the power grid: transformers, switchgear and the gear that moves electricity at high voltage. It is a focused bet on grid upgrades driven by data centers and electrification, a picks-and-shovels play on the power buildout.
JPAN: Japanese companies picked actively by Asia specialists: electronics and chip firms, industrial exporters, banks and consumer brands. It is a single-country fund offering a manager's best ideas in the world's third-largest stock market, with returns also moved by the yen.
KPO: Options that create stock exposure to both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 at once, while selling other options for premium income and partial protection. It tries to keep a portion of two indexes' upside with a softer landing in declines, a middle path between owning stocks and sitting out.
LUMA: Companies that make technology from light: lasers, fiber-optic gear, optical sensors and the photonics inside chips and self-driving systems. It is a narrow, deep-tech bet on light-based hardware, far more specialized than a general semiconductor fund, so its fortunes hinge on a handful of suppliers.
MGIN: Infrastructure assets from around the world: toll roads, airports, pipelines, power networks and phone towers, mostly held as listed companies. These businesses collect steady fees from things everyone uses, so the fund aims for reliable income and moderate growth with less drama than most stock funds.
MINY: Mining companies focused on strategic metals, the materials behind batteries, defense and clean tech, paired with an options program that turns their swings into income. It blends a commodity growth bet with regular payouts, though selling options caps some of the miners' upside in a metal price boom.
MULT: Bonds from nearly every corner of the market: government and corporate debt, bank loans, and mortgage and asset-backed securities, from the US and abroad. Managers roam across sectors hunting for the best income, making it a flexible core bond holding that takes more credit risk than a plain government fund.
MUNG: Municipal bonds arranged in a ladder aimed at the year 2046, paying tax-free interest and gradually returning principal through regular distributions. It is built for savers who want a bond portfolio that pays itself out over time toward a distant goal, with federal tax-free income along the way.
MUNH: Municipal bonds arranged in a ladder aimed at the year 2056, paying tax-free interest and gradually returning principal through regular distributions. With three decades to run it behaves more like a long-term bond holding than its shorter cousins, suiting very long goals that want federal tax-free income.
PCOV: Dividend-paying US stocks across technology, banking, health care and industry, paired with an options program that adds premium income on top of the dividends. It is an equity income holding that trades some upside for two income streams, so it should lag in roaring markets and cushion mild ones.
PMJN: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb as much loss as the structure allows over a one-year period ending in June, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is the most defensive version of a buffer fund, suiting investors who fear a down year more than they want full upside.
QOWZ: US companies with a record of steadily growing free cash flow, the cash left after running and investing in the business, led by technology at two-thirds. It screens for financial strength and consistency rather than hype, making it a quality-tilted growth holding.
RECI: A core portfolio of large US stocks, tilted by Columbia's research, plus an options overlay that sells calls to add premium income. It tries to behave like a core stock holding with a steadier income stream on top, giving up some upside in strong rallies to collect those premiums.
RMRC: US stocks held through funds for each of the S&P 500's industries, with managers shifting the weights and able to turn defensive when risk rises. It aims to keep most of the stock market's growth while stepping aside in deeper trouble, a core holding with a hand on the brake.
RND: Companies that pour money back into research and development, led by technology at nearly half, with health care and consumer innovators behind. The bet is that heavy research spending today becomes tomorrow's growth, making it a close cousin of other innovation funds with a spending-based screen.
SMCP: Mid-sized companies from the US and abroad that trade on US exchanges, with an unusual tilt toward miners, energy firms and regional banks. It is an actively picked mid-cap holding that leans into commodity-driven industries, so it behaves differently from the tech-heavy funds that dominate this size range.
SPAQ: Special purpose acquisition companies, the blank-check firms that raise cash first and go hunting for a business to buy later. Managers pick the deals they think will land well, so it is a speculator's corner of the market where outcomes range from dull to dramatic.
SPCI: Space industry companies, rocket builders, satellite operators and their suppliers, combined with a systematic put-selling program that generates income. It pairs a speculative growth theme with an options income engine, so payouts come with the sharp swings of a young, contract-driven industry.
SSCP: Small companies from the US and abroad that trade on US exchanges, picked actively across banks, manufacturers, technology and energy. Small caps can outgrow big stocks over time but swing much harder, and this one's active, all-sector approach makes it a stock-picker's bet.
TDNA: Biotechnology companies working on new medicines made from living cells, from gene therapies to cancer and rare-disease drugs. Biotech is a hit-driven business where one trial result can double or halve a stock overnight, so this is among the swingiest corners of health care.
TIPB: Inflation-linked bonds, mainly Treasury TIPS, arranged in a ladder aimed at 2035 and paying out interest plus gradual principal along the way. It is designed to protect purchasing power toward a specific future year, trading higher yields elsewhere for a government-backed inflation adjustment.
TSEE: Small US companies below the Russell 2000's size ceiling, picked across health care, banking, industry and energy by the firm's analysts. It is an active small-cap holding where the growth can be strong and the swings sharp, since small companies have thinner trading and shakier finances than giants.
TSOL: Direct ownership of SOL, the token of the Solana blockchain, held by a trust and priced once a day. It wraps one fast, cheap-transaction cryptocurrency in a stock-market fund, so expect large daily swings driven purely by crypto sentiment, with no staking income on top.
USG: Gold exposure through futures and exchange warrants, paired with an income strategy that sells options against the position. It keeps gold's role as a crisis hedge while trying to pay some income along the way, something plain gold funds never do.
USNG: US companies that move and store natural gas: pipeline operators, storage and export terminals, and the builders behind them. It is an energy infrastructure bet that lives on gas volumes and shipping fees rather than the gas price alone, aiming for steadier income than oil and gas producers offer.
XBTY: An income strategy built on options tied to a leveraged bitcoin fund rather than on bitcoin itself. It sells options to capture the rich premiums that crypto's wild swings create, aiming for large payouts while taking amplified losses in a bitcoin sell-off.
XCNY: Emerging-market companies everywhere except China: Taiwanese chipmakers, Indian banks and tech firms, and miners and manufacturers across Asia and Latin America. It keeps the growth story of developing markets while removing the single biggest country, a choice many investors now want on its own.
XCSH: Combinations of options called box spreads, which behave like short-term loans and are rolled over every few weeks to mimic Treasury bills. It aims to earn a little more than T-bills while staying cash-like, with returns coming from options pricing instead of government debt.
XLFI: Banks, insurers, brokers and payment companies from the S&P 500, paired with an options program that adds premium income. Financial stocks already pay healthy dividends, so this stacks a second income stream on top, while staying fully exposed to a sector that swings with interest rates and credit fears.
YFYA: A ready-made mix of other income funds, holding short-term bonds, preferred shares and similar payout vehicles chosen for yield. It plays the cash-plus role, aiming to pay more than a money market fund with modest price movement, though the layered funds mean two sets of fees.
